19943-the-hippodrome:
Rachel Hayward's The Hippodrome, dated 1913, is a novel of the music-hall world. Its manager counts women only for their money or brains, the narrator observes. If women had cash to spend, that was a different matter. Brains and energies that could be used counted too. As women themselves, they did not count in his career. The cold eye of that portrait drives the book.

The Hippodrome was a famous London variety theater's name. Hayward sets ambition and exploitation under its lights. Performers, managers, and hangers-on fill her stage. The novel treats show business as business first. Its cynicism feels modern beside period romance. It survives as a sharp theatrical novel.
20116-the-belief-in-immortality-and-the-:
J. G. Frazer wrote The Belief in Immortality and the Worship of the Dead, a vast study of faith. This volume deals much with beliefs in Australia, among other lands. It lists what Queensland peoples held about the soul and the dead. Some held that the dead are born again in new bodies.

Others held that the dead go to the sky or a far land. Frazer sorts such beliefs from reports sent from across the world. His method compares customs side by side on a huge scale. Readers get a landmark of early anthropology, rich in detail and bold claims.
20133-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-at-:
Laura Lee Hope published Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue at Aunt Lu's City Home in 1916. Bunny wakes and laughs as he rubs his sleepy eyes awake. He jokes that Sue thinks they are back on grandpa's farm. Their mother stands smiling at the two children in the hall.

City life gives Bunny and Sue new sights at every turn. Aunt Lu's home brings traffic, shops, and crowds unlike their small town. The Bunny Brown books follow the pair through mild scrapes and bright days. Young readers get gentle fun, family warmth, and a child's view of the city.
20293-a-popular-history-of-the-art-of-mu:
W. S. B. Mathews wrote A Popular History of the Art of Music. He aims to cover the same span that fills far larger histories. Naumann, Ambros, and Fétis used three to ten times the space. Mathews grants that competent judges will differ on his success.

Specimens of music and many engravings help the reader hear and see. The book runs from the earliest times to the composer's own day. It made music history plain to students and keen amateurs alike. Readers get a brisk, well-stocked tour of Western music in one volume.
20464-a-journey-through-france-in-war-ti:
Joseph G. Butler, Jr. toured France in 1917 as part of an American commission, and his book reports what he saw. The chapters move from the front to hospitals and cities. Photographs show the commissioners and a typical French soldier in uniform.

Later chapters describe the Carrel method of treating wounds. Another follows a city caught in an army's path. The contents run to twenty-six chapters in all. Butler closes with his impressions of France and the French people. The book gave American readers a businessman's eyewitness account of their new ally at war.
20559-r-holmes-co-being-the-remarkable-a:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote R. Holmes and Co. as a comic answer to Sherlock Holmes and the gentleman thief Raffles. His hero, Raffles Holmes, is the son of Holmes and the daughter of Raffles. He solves cases with a thief's talents and a detective's brain, and keeps the profits vague.

The narrator suffers through a New York heat wave. Even the radiators, cold all winter, now hiss at the touch of a moistened finger. Enough cooling drinks to float an ocean liner have passed into him, with no effect. Bangs's parodies were best sellers in their day.
20632-molly-brown-s-orchard-home:
Nell Speed's Molly Brown's Orchard Home, published in 1915, belongs to her Molly Brown series for girls. Molly and her friends plan a stay at an orchard home, away from their usual college and Kentucky scenes. The trip begins under a cloud, as Molly explains in her letter home.

Our going is not quite so happy as we meant it to be. Kent cannot come with us as we had planned. He will have to stay in Louisville for some months, and may not be able to leave at all this winter. Some complication of their affairs keeps him. The girls go on without him.
20907-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Sages from all Greece stream to Sardis at its height in this classic prose piece. Solon of Athens stands among them before rich King Croesus of Lydia. The Best of the World's Classics gathers such peaks of prose in one set.

Henry Cabot Lodge edited this ten-volume store of great writing in 1909. Herodotus here tells how Solon warned Croesus not to call any man happy till death. Tales, essays, speeches, and histories span the whole set. It served homes that wanted the world's best prose, well chosen and handsomely bound, within one shelf's reach.
21038-a-dog-with-a-bad-name:
Dry rot eats Bolsover College from within in A Dog with a Bad Name. Years of slow decay, Reed writes, have left patching near hopeless there. Boys expelled and masters resigned mark the school's vain tries at cure.

A boy with a bad name, fairly or not, stands at the tale's sore centre. School honour, false blame, and grit fill Reed's plot with real stakes. He asks how a name sticks and what it costs to clear one. Among his school tales, this one cuts deepest, a story of reputation in a world where boys judge fast and forgive slow.
21227-shenac-s-work-at-home:
Margaret Murray Robertson opens with sorrow in a Scottish district long ago, when many families were driven from homes held for generations. Most chose to cross the ocean and build new homes in a strange world beyond the sea. Shenac's story grows from that leaving of Scotland.

The emigrants left kirks, graves, and kin behind, facing weeks or months on the water with little knowledge of the land ahead. Robertson follows what such families made of Canada, and how a young woman like Shenac could work for her home from inside it. Faith, endurance, and household duty carry the tale, as in her other Scottish Canadian stories.
21345-a-wounded-name:
Captain Charles King was a career army officer and prolific novelist of the frontier army. He opens in a dust cloud on the alkali flats, as a stagecoach lurches toward Sancho's ranch. Sancho keeps a dinner ranch and watches through a fine binocular for passengers, with the boy Pedro announcing every cloud of dust. A disgraced officer's arrival starts the tale.

The title quotes Shakespeare: poor wounded name, my bosom as a bed shall lodge thee. King builds his plot on an officer's ruined reputation and its slow repair among soldiers, prospectors, and ranch folk in the West. His own service at West Point and on campaign gave his army tales their easy authority.
21562-the-gulf-and-inland-waters-the-nav:
A. T. Mahan tells the naval war on the Gulf and the rivers in The Gulf and Inland Waters, copyrighted in 1883. The book is volume three of The Navy in the Civil War. Mahan, a serving captain, built his tale chiefly on official reports.

Where reports left gaps, he wrote to men who had been there and asked. River fleets, blockade work, and the taking of ports fill the narrative. New Orleans, Mobile, and the Mississippi campaigns stand at its heart. Mahan later won world fame for his books on sea power, and this crisp, early history shows the mind at work.
21625-play-the-game:
Honor Carmody likes the boys, and owns it, in Ruth Comfort Mitchell's Play the Game! The book was copyrighted in 1920 and issued in book form by Appleton. Honor's mother and stepfather plan to send her to Marlborough school in Los Angeles.

Honor is aghast, sure she could not bear a girls' school. Mrs Lorimer, her friend's mother, is lovely and girlish at forty-one, with six children. She warns against letting a girl be queer, in the talk of the day. Mitchell, who also wrote verse tales, builds a bright tale of school, sport, and young love.
21629-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Volume two of The Best of the World's Classics, restricted to prose, treats Rome from 234 B.C. to 180 A.D. Henry Cabot Lodge leads the editing, with Francis W. Halsey as his partner. Portraits of Marcus Aurelius, Caesar, Cicero, and Seneca front the book, issued in 1909.

Cato the Censor opens with rules for running a Roman farm. Cicero follows with essays on old age, friendship, and duty, and a letter on his daughter's death. Notes explain each writer's life and place. The ten-volume set aimed to give home readers the cream of world prose in sound translations.
21679-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Volume three of The Best of the World's Classics, restricted to prose, covers Great Britain and Ireland from 1281 to 1745. Henry Cabot Lodge and Francis W. Halsey edit the set, issued in 1909. Milton, Bacon, Chaucer, and Shakespeare stand pictured at the front.

Richard de Bury opens with In Praise of Books, from his Philobiblon. De Bury, bishop of Durham and chancellor of England, founded a library at Oxford. Mandeville's travels and Wyclif's gospel rendering follow, then Chaucer on riches. Notes give each writer's life and place, in a home library of the world's best prose.
21877-woodrow-wilson-and-the-world-war-a:
America under Wilson is chronicled in Charles Seymour's Woodrow Wilson and the World War, a 1921 volume in the Yale Chronicles of America series. Seymour begins on March 4, 1913, when Wilson entered the White House as the first Democratic president elected in twenty years. No one, he says, could have guessed the part Wilson would play. Chapters follow neutrality, the submarine crisis, plots and preparedness, and America's decision for war.

The home front and the fighting front each get their due before the path to peace. The peace conference, the League of Nations fight, and the Senate's rejection of the treaty close the tale. Seymour wrote as a scholar close to events. The book remains a clear, early history of America's Great War years.
21890-the-path-to-home:
Home, fathers, and small daily kindnesses fill Edgar A. Guest's The Path to Home, a book of poems published in 1919. Guest was America's best-loved newspaper poet, author of Just Folks and A Heap o' Livin'. The index alone maps his world: Daddies, His Dog, The Cookie-Lady, Bread and Jam, and Becoming a Dad. Even the famous It Couldn't Be Done is here.

Guest writes in plain rhyme about mothers at doorways, children at gates, and asters along the fence. War touches the book too, in An Apple Tree in France and At the Peace Table. His secret was simple: he praised the ordinary home as the best place on earth. Millions of readers agreed, and cut his verses from the papers to keep.
22102-the-hills-of-home:
Alfred Coppel wrote The Hills of Home as a pulp science fiction adventure. His hero Jimmy shifts a heavy Martian pistol to his left hand and checks his harness. He is well armed, and he has no fear of the Plant Men. Barefoot, he turns upstream toward the shallows where he can cross the river.

Beyond the crossing lies his search along the base of the Golden Cliffs. A phonograph's sound floats over the water from the enemy side. Coppel mixes Mars, jungle peril, and a boyish hero in the magazine manner. The tale is pure pulp: quick scenes, strange creatures, and a young Earthman at home in an alien wilderness.
22153-pagan-and-christian-rome:
Rodolfo Lanciani, the great archaeologist of Rome, wrote Pagan and Christian Rome, issued in English in 1892. Lanciani had directed excavations across the city for years. His book moves between two Romes that share the same streets. One plate shows the graves found around the tomb of St. Peter, drawn from a rare engraving by the Pope's master mason.

Lanciani describes temples turned into churches, martyrs' shrines, and catacombs. He writes as a digger who knew the soil layer by layer. Tourists and scholars both used his books as guides to the ruins. This volume remains a vivid record of Rome's archaeology in its heroic age.
22184-more-tales-in-the-land-of-nursery-:
More Tales in the Land of Nursery Rhyme continues a series that sends children into the country where rhymes live. In this scene, delicate foreign birds have been sheltered in a barn through bad weather. The home birds despise them as foreigners. The strangers crouch shyly in a corner, silent unless spoken to, while a cold English winter beats outside.

Around such episodes the tales weave Mother Goose figures into small adventures. The land of nursery rhyme works like a storybook map: every rhyme a place to visit. Ada M. Marzials and her collaborators made the series for children who already knew the rhymes by heart. This volume adds fresh tales to the first collection's world.
22193-an-englishwoman-s-home:
An Englishwoman's Home, published in 1918, is a novel in letters from the last year of the Great War. It opens with a cedar wood box: the writer can see her friend's puzzled brows over so simple a note. Why should opening a box count as a wartime event? The letters answer slowly, through the small happenings of a home under war's shadow.

Domestic detail carries the book: houses, servants, rationed comforts, and news from the front. The writer chronicles a private world the war keeps shaking. Letter novels suited such intimate records well. This one preserves an Englishwoman's home front in 1918 from inside the household itself.
22374-caw-caw-or-the-chronicle-of-crows-:
Caw Caw, or the Chronicle of Crows, tells a spring-time tale in verse. Its subjects are a patient pair of crows. For many weeks, the poem says, they seek no other occupation.

One crow sits and looks around the woods. The other makes the woods resound with loud cawings. He brings worms, seeds, and other good things home. Kindly, he feeds his brooding mate from early morning to late evening. The poem watches nest life with fond, comic care. Readers get a gentle animal story in rhyme. It turns two common birds into a devoted pair worth following through spring.
22381-myths-and-legends-of-ancient-greec:
Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome retells the old gods' stories for general readers. Its second portion paints a picture of old Greek life. Customs, superstitions, and princely hospitalities fill that part of the work.

Those Greek-life chapters run longer than is usual in such books. The writer thought daily life deserved room beside the myths. Readers thus get tales plus the world that told them. Feasts, homes, and beliefs stand behind the gods and heroes. The book served schools and homes as a first mythology. It still gives a clear, story-first entry into Greek and Roman legend, with manners attached.
22654-the-doctor-of-pimlico-being-the-di:
The Doctor of Pimlico, subtitled Being the Disclosure of a Great Crime, is a crime novel by William Le Queux, the popular writer of thrillers and spy tales. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title promises a respectable London district hiding a dark secret, a Le Queux specialty.

The sample shows four men walking together: a sharp, grey-haired general with many war ribbons, a tall staff captain in Gordon Highlanders tartan, and two civilians in shooting jackets. Soldiers and sportsmen side by side hint at the military circle the crime will touch. The book delivers period melodrama: hidden guilt, careful disguises, and a slow disclosure. It suits readers of early British crime fiction.
22716-the-book-hunter-at-home:
The Book Hunter at Home is a companion volume of essays on book collecting and the pleasures of the hunt. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its hunter has grown older since his earlier adventures among London's shops, and now writes from his own shelves.

It is a sad truth, the book opens, that bargains come oftener in youth than in age. The sophist may argue that age breeds philosophy, and philosophy scorns worldly things. Yet the book-hunter, among the most philosophical of beings, hunts bargains until his career's very end. Anecdotes of finds, prices, and fellow collectors fill the pages. The tone is club-room mellow, written for readers who measure wealth in shelf feet.
22916-left-at-home:
Mary L. Code sets Left at Home in a pleasant room on a winter's evening. Frost shines clear and cold outside while a bright fire blazes within, lighting the crimson carpet and curtains. On the snowy table-cover stand preparations for tea, of the kind Arthur usually appreciates at this hour. The subtitle calls the tale the heart's resting-place.

Domestic fiction of this kind built its drama from absence, duty, and reunion at the fireside. Someone has been left at home, and the story weighs what home asks of those who keep it. Code writes in the warm, moral register her readers expected. The result is a quiet period tale, best read for its household detail and its faith in ordinary affection.
22960-among-the-pines-or-south-in-secess:
Edmund Kirke travels Among the Pines, in the South in secession time, with a colonel and the colonel's servant Jim. Jim, about thirty, was born and raised in his master's family. The party journeys by day where possible, stopping at night at convenient resting places, the colonel, Jim, and the narrator in the same or adjoining rooms.

Kirke, the pen name of James Roberts Gilmore, wrote to show Northern readers the wartime South from inside. Plantations, poor whites, and enslaved people all enter his sketches, filtered through a Union man's eyes. The book's scenes of travel carry its politics quietly. It remains a vivid, arguable piece of wartime reporting, best read as one witness's South rather than the whole of it.
23117-the-island-home:
A sailor's song opens The Island Home. The opening song praises a following breeze, a full white sail, and a mast bending bravely under it. Our palace is the stout wooden ship, the chorus boasts, and our inheritance the open sea.

Behind the song stands a tale of the sea and of home made on an island, in the tradition of the Robinsonade. Richard Archer's island story, as it is often credited, sends its company through wreck, settlement, and return. Sea songs like the opening set the book's weather, hearty and homesick at once. Readers who like castaway industry, huts raised and gardens planted against the wild, will find the familiar pleasures honestly served.
23127-julian-home:
Prize day glitters in Julian Home. Harton families spend the morning touring school and village. Mothers and sisters wander in delight while their young escorts point out the sights with pride. Some cross the cricket field, others take the pleasant path down toward the bathing place.

Frederic William Farrar wrote Julian Home as a tale of college life, the university answer to his famous school story Eric. Undergraduates, examinations, friendships, and temptations fill its terms. The prize-day opening shows the world at its sunniest, families touring the ground their sons must make good in. Farrar's earnestness governs the whole, a Victorian clergyman's view of youth, affectionate and forever on the watch for the first wrong step.
23264-the-settlers-at-home:
The Settlers at Home opens by placing its scene with care. The land in question is not an island in the sea, the book explains. It is part of Lincolnshire: a tract hilly at its centre and ringed by rivers on most sides.

The Trent runs along its east side. Smaller rivers once ran round the rest and met the Humber northward. That ring of water shapes the settlers' world: cut off, yet connected. Readers get a story of home settlement in the Lincolnshire fens, where water, land, and isolation decide how a community lives.
23276-the-white-rose-of-langley-a-story-:
The White Rose of Langley is a story of the olden time, about a woman worn down by her life. Hard work and exposure have marked her, and sorrow may have marked her too. She sits up and looks wearily over the winter scene spread out before her.

Her voice holds none of a child's querulous complaint. Instead there is the dull, sullen apathy of hopeless endurance. That tone sets the tale's mood at once. Readers get a historical story of endurance under hardship, where winter, labour, and quiet suffering stand in for speeches about fate.
a-second-home: Balzac's 1842 story of a young woman who finds a second home and a second chance at happiness. Tender and quietly moving, it shows his sympathy for the overlooked. A gentle tale from the Human Comedy.
adam-eve-pinch-me: Adam and Eve and Pinch Me, A, e, coppard's stories, the pinch tales. This book preserves that collection. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
anne-bradstreet-and-her-time: Helen Campbell tells the life of Anne Bradstreet — America's first published poet — against the backdrop of Puritan New England. Her verses, written in a wilderness settlement, gave voice to faith, family, and a woman's mind. A warm biography of a remarkable pioneer of American letters.
antonina-or-the-fall-of-rome: Antonina, or The Fall of Rome, Wilkie Collins's historical novel. The empire's fall. This book preserves that tale. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
back-home: Eugene Wood's Back Home: a novel of returning to one's roots. Warm and nostalgic in the popular style. A pleasant story of homecoming. Wood's homecoming is every reader's own, every reader's own homecoming, warm and nostalgic.
beauty-and-the-beast-and-tales-of-home: This collection gathers Beauty and the Beast with home tales. Enchantment teaches. The Tower library holds the full text. It beautied beasts. Roses bloomed. Love transformed. Homes warmed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
brought-home: Stretton's tale brings its wanderer home at last. The homecoming carries the story's moral weight. A Victorian children's story. Its contents inform the historical record. The book preserves that tale. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abel-place-na: A 1913 entry on Abel as a place name — several meadows and mourning-places in old Canaan. Anthony Maas maps each biblical mention. Abel-meholah, Abel-mizraim, and the rest find their sites. Geography for Bible readers. Each meadow of mourning keeps its biblical story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-henri-: This 1913 reference article on Alfred Mame — the great Catholic publisher of Tours. Georges Goyau honors his press. His books carried faith to millions. The Maison Mame became an institution. A printer apostle of France. His missals filled the French churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angouleme: A 1913 entry on Angoulême — the French diocese of the Charente. Georges Goyau gives its history. Its domed cathedral crowns the hill. The Valois counts ruled its lands. A see of western France. Its paper mills served the printers. Its ramparts ring the old town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-ansel: This 1913 reference piece on Antoine Anselme — a French preacher of note. John Joseph A'Becket records his career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His sermons edified the faithful. A voice in the Church's pulpit. His Advent station drew the court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerical-cost: This 1913 reference article on clerical costume — the priest's distinctive dress. Herbert Thurston traces its sober forms. The cassock marks the sacred calling. The collar bespeaks the Roman priest. The livery of the Church's ministers. Its biretta crowns the learned head.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-and-c: A 1913 entry on the Anima — the German college and church in Rome. August Joseph Schmidlin honors its ancient hospice. The pilgrims of the Empire found rest. The Borgo keeps its national church. The home of the German nation. Its Santa Maria dell'Anima is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyme: A 1913 entry on Cyme — the Aeolian city, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Asian shore. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dome: This 1913 reference article on the dome — the church's crowning vault. Thomas Poole explains its soaring art. The Pantheon's eye lights the vast round. The Renaissance crowned the new St. Peter's. The cupola of the sacred building. Its Brunelleschi dome is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-: This 1913 reference piece on the Holy Name — the January feast. Frederick Holweck unfolds its Franciscan origin. Bernardine spread the sacred monogram. The Church honors the saving Name. The feast of the IHS devotion. Its January second is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-v: This 1913 reference article on Geoffrey of Vendôme — the abbot-cardinal. Francis Schaefer notes his famous letters. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the twelfth century. A prelate of the reforming age. His 1132 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-balme: This 1913 reference piece on Balme — an English priest of note. Andrew Egan records his career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His zeal served the nineteenth century. A pastor among the clergy. His 1890 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-impediment-of: A 1913 entry on the impediment of crime — the marriage bar. Richard Burtsell unfolds the canonical kinds. Adultery blocks the guilty vows. The Church guards the seemly bounds. The diriment of the murderous plot. Its 1917 Code is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-college: A 1913 entry on the Irish College in Rome — the exiles' seminary. Michael O'Riordan honors its famous house. Ludovisi founded the holy school. The priests bless the training years. The college of the Irish exiles. Its 1628 founding is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois: A 1913 entry on Saint-Cosme — the Mississippi missionary. James Mooney recounts his martyr's tale. The Natchez claimed the fearless priest. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-joseph-g: This 1913 reference piece on Gaume — the French controversialist. Pierre Auguste Fournet honors his famous works. His pen scourged the pagan classics. The faithful prized the fearless voice. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1879 death is famed. His 1879 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-libera-me: A 1913 entry on the Libera Me — the absolution's chant. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its solemn use. The choir pleads the dead's release. The Church keeps the hallowed words. The requiem marks its place. Its Gregorian chant is famed. Its 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany-of-the: This 1913 reference piece on the Litany of the Holy Name — the Jesus invocations. Francis Mershman unfolds its devout use. The faithful chant the Savior's titles. The Church keeps the hallowed form. The devout love its music. Its 1862 approval is famed. Its 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-rene-vi: A 1913 entry on Villermé — the French physician. Georges Goyau honors his famous hygiene. His science probed the workers' ills. The Academy prized its learned son. The clinics keep his name. His 1863 death is famed. His 1863 hygiene is famed. His 1863 public health is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-psau: This biographical entry profiles Nicholas Psaume, a French bishop of the 1500s, tracing his episcopate and his service to the Church as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of prelates, preserved among its records of French bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicole-oresme: Nicole Oresme was the bishop-scholar who anticipated modern economics, criticized astrology, and translated Aristotle into French. This entry covers his career, his science, and his influence. The medieval mind that saw the future: his economics preceded Adam Smith by centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de: Molesme was the Burgundian abbey where St. Robert began the reform that became Cîteaux and the Cistercian order. This entry traces its history, its abbots, and its legacy. The cradle of the white monks: Robert left it to found the New Monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oriflamme: The Oriflamme was the red banner of St. Denis that French kings carried into battle. This entry traces its history, its legend, and its last unfurling. The sacred war-flag of France: its red silk flew over the fields of Bouvines and Agincourt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philibert-de-: Philibert de l'Orme was the Renaissance architect of the Tuileries and the French classical style. This entry covers his career, his buildings, and his treatises. The Vitruvius of France: his great Tuileries palace defined the classical French style for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prime: Prime is the first little hour of the Divine Office. This entry explains its psalms, its history, and its place. The morning's first prayer: its short psalms greet the rising dawn each morning in monastic choir stalls worldwide in song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-creator: Rerum Creator optime is the Monday hymn of Lauds. This entry explains its text, its author, and its music. The hymn of the week's beginning: its ancient notes greet the dawn on Monday's Lauds in choir and chapel and cell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rome: Rome is the Eternal City of the popes. This very long entry treats its history, its churches, and its monuments. The capital of the Catholic world: its golden domes crown the hills of Latium in the sun of Italy's heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salome: Salome was the daughter of Herodias. This entry examines her dance, her request, and her fate. The dancer of the Baptist's death: her wicked dance cost a head in Machaerus' hall in the 30s A.D. of the Tetrarch Herod Antipas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-sister: The School Sisters of Notre Dame are the teachers of Bavaria's foundress. This entry covers their rule, their schools, and their world. The sisters of the classroom: their many schools dot the world in the 1800s' decades of the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th: The Society of the Holy Name is the Dominicans' confraternity. This entry covers its chapters, its members, and its history. The men of the sacred Name: their many chapters dot the parishes in the 1270s' order in the provinces of the friars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agnes-of-r: St. Agnes of Rome was the martyr of the Via Nomentana. This entry traces her passion, her lambs, and her cult. The virgin of the Roman winter: her blessed lambs graced January in the basilica of the saint in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o: St. Eusebius of Rome was the confessor of the Arian age. This entry traces his constancy, his exile, and his cult. The priest of the Roman church: his brave constancy crowned the 350s in the city of the popes in the church.

elinor-wyllys-or-the-young-folk-of-longb: Susan Fenimore Cooper's 1846 novel, volume one: the young folk of Longbridge and their village world. The first American novel of domestic realism, gentle and observant. A pioneering work, unjustly neglected. Cooper's village of Longbridge is Cooperstown idealized, and lovely for it.
for-name-and-fame: For Name and Fame, G. A. Henty's Afghan War tale. The fame seekers. This book preserves that adventure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
going-some: Rex Beach trades his usual northern adventure for comedy in this lighthearted novel. A pampered young athlete is challenged to prove himself in the rough world of the West, with hilarious and romantic results. Beach's high spirits carry the story along — a fun change of pace from the king of the adventure novel.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADomesticInte:
Covert Action: Threat to the Constitution came from the Center for National Security Studies, a project of the Fund for Peace. The Center had been founded to watch the watchers, and this publication states its core argument in its title.

It holds that secret operations abroad corrode constitutional government at home, the thesis the oversight movement pressed through the 1970s. The Center's staff worked the fights over domestic spying, and its publications armed congressional reformers with arguments and documents. The piece is advocacy literature from the Church Committee era, preserved complete for readers of that movement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
Joel Sappell reported for the Herald Examiner on a charge with a twist in it. The Citizens' Commission on Police Repression, a group formed to fight police spying, accused the Los Angeles Police Department of spying on the group itself. The department's Public Disorder and Intelligence Division, the charge said, had infiltrated the coalition in 1978.

The case captures the strange loop of domestic intelligence work in that era. A citizens' watchdog said the watched had become the watchers' target. Sappell's article preserves the accusation as the commission made it, part of a wider fight over police intelligence in Los Angeles.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBICrime_FBI_Cr:
James Vorenberg assessed the Nixon administration's war on crime in an article titled The War on Crime: The First Five Years. His review reaches back to the report of the President's Commission on Law Enforcement, whose findings set the terms of the fight. Five years on, he measured what the campaign had actually done.

Vorenberg writes as a legal scholar grading a political promise. Law-and-order pledges had won elections, and his article asks what they bought in practice. It is a period judgment on federal crime policy, made by a writer close to the commission whose work began the era.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OswaldsGameJean:
Jean Davison's book 'Oswald's Game' is preserved here as a full-text scan. Davison studied Lee Harvey Oswald's writings, politics, and movements, and built her account from that record. The scan's front matter, including the ISBN page, is garbled in the character recognition, but the book itself is present in full.

Davison's title borrows Oswald's own habit of treating politics as moves in a game. Her book stands apart from both the lone-gunman briefs and the conspiracy literature in one way: it takes Oswald's stated beliefs seriously as motives. Readers get a complete study of the accused assassin as a political actor, written from his papers and the testimony of people who knew him.
heart-and-science-a-story-of-the-present: Heart and Science, a story of the present time by Wilkie Collins. The heart versus science. This book preserves that novel. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
key-out-of-time:
Key Out of Time is a science fiction novel by Andre Norton, copyrighted in 1963 by the World Publishing Company. Its contents promise eleven chapters, from The Lotus World to Weapon from the Depths. Ross Murdock and his companions face storm menace, ancient mariners, and a time wreck. Loketh the Useless and witches' meat appear among the chapter titles.

Norton's Time Traders books send agents into alien worlds and lost pasts. Here the crew lands among free rovers and baldies on a watery planet. A lair of Mano-Nui and death at Kyn Add raise the stakes late in the book. This copy is a second printing, cleared under a noted textual rule. Norton builds fast adventure on time travel and first contact.
lays-of-ancient-rome:
Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote the ballads in Lays of Ancient Rome. Famous lays include Horatius, Virginia, and the Battle of Lake Regillus. A long preface argues that early Roman history is largely fable.

Public records perished when the Gauls burned Rome, Macaulay notes. Poets, not clerks, kept the old stories alive after that loss. His ballads rebuild those lost songs in bold English verse. Horatius holding the bridge became a schoolroom favorite for generations. The lays mix scholarship, patriotism, and stirring storytelling. Schoolchildren once learned Horatius by heart across Britain. Its ringing refrain helped fix Rome's heroes in common memory.
led-astray-and-the-sphinx-two-novellas-i:
Octave Feuillet's two novellas, Led Astray and The Sphinx, share one volume. Street and Smith copyrighted this edition in 1891. Feuillet had won fame with Romance of a Poor Young Man.

Led Astray opens with a letter from George to Paul in Paris. George writes at nine in the evening from Rozel. His friend has just arrived home from Germany. A graphic description, the chapter title promises, will follow. Feuillet builds refined French society tales from such letters and confessions. Two novellas let Feuillet contrast two kinds of love. Both turn on letters, secrets, and wounded pride.
lha-dhu-or-the-dark-day-the-works-of-wil:
William Carleton's tale Lha Dhu, or The Dark Day, appears in his collected works. The story opens by praising Ireland's softly shaded landscape. Valleys, glens, meadows, and hamlets scatter across the green island, he writes.

Each valley holds some tearful memory of humble calamity, he says. The proud world never hears those small sorrows. Carleton devotes his fiction to exactly those hidden griefs. His peasants are moved by mirth and sorrow in equal force. The Dark Day tells one such humble, haunting Irish story. Carleton knew Irish peasant life from his own youth. That knowledge gives even his legends a lived weight.
libretto-la-bohe-me:
Giacomo Puccini's opera La Bohème rests on this libretto by Giacosa and Illica. W. Grist and P. Pinkerton supplied the English version printed here. The story comes from Henri Murger's book about bohemian life in Paris. Four acts follow poor young artists around the Latin Quarter near 1830.

Rudolph the poet and Marcel the painter share a freezing attic studio. They burn a rejected manuscript for warmth and joke through their poverty. Mimi and Musetta bring love, and later sorrow, into their circle. The libretto lets English readers follow every word of the famous opera.
love-and-life-an-old-story-in-eighteenth:
Love and Life, printed in 1880, is a novel by Charlotte M. Yonge in eighteenth-century dress. Its chapters open with a syllabub party at the House of Delavie. A summons follows, then an enchanted castle and a dark chamber. A voice from the grave deepens the mystery at the heart of the tale.

Yonge tells an old story of love tested by strangeness and separation. Her heroine must trust a husband she rarely sees plainly. Windsor clergy, a queen of beauty, and country manners fill out the world. The book mixes fairy-tale wonder with the rules of real society. It rewards readers who like gentle, old-fashioned romance.
madame-chrysanthe-me:
Madame Chrysanthème is Pierre Loti's diary-novel of a summer in Japan. Laura Ensor translated this Modern Library edition into English. Loti swears he changed nothing in his diary, not even the dates. He names the three chief persons: myself, Japan, and Japan's effect on me.

Loti was a French naval officer stationed at Nagasaki. There he entered a temporary marriage with a young Japanese woman. Chrysanthème, his bride, shares his house for one season. His pages record temples, fans, boats, and his own restless moods. The book charmed Europe and fed the later Madame Butterfly story. It remains a famous, uneasy portrait of Japan through foreign eyes.
making-the-house-a-home:
Making the House a Home is Edgar A. Guest's memoir of family life, dated 1922. A verse at the front promises smiles, tears, weal, and woe. Guest says he and his wife have been building a home for fifteen years. A house takes months, he notes, but a home takes years.

They married on June 28, 1906, when he was twenty-five. He had just left his job as a Detroit Free Press police reporter. Page by page he tells of children, work, grief, and small joys. Guest was America's beloved newspaper poet of home and kindness. This plain, warm record shows the life behind his verses.
marjorie-s-maytime:
Marjorie's Maytime is a Carolyn Wells story for girls, dated 1911. It opens with a May party for Marjorie Maynard. A new pet and a trial trip follow in quick order. The children visit a camp and find Marjorie held a captive.

Two grandmothers take their turns: Grandma Sherwood and Grandma Maynard. An escapade, an exciting picnic, and some ancient finery fill the spring. There are calls at the schoolhouse and a merry joke. A ride in May and a trip to the circus crown the season. Little Vivian and a Boston visit close the book. Wells keeps every chapter sunny and brisk.
master-skylark-a-story-of-shakspere-s-ti:
John Bennett wrote Master Skylark, a tale of Shakespeare's time. Reginald B. Birch drew the pictures for the book. A note gives the hero's mother a place of honor at the front.

Nicholas Attwood, the skylark of the title, sings for the Lord Admiral's men. Chapters track him from home to Coventry and the Warwick road. He is disowned, rides for freedom, and reaches London town. At the end he sings before Queen Elizabeth at Christmas time. The Rose play house and the Children of Paul's show London's stage world. A new life and a waning year lead toward the Queen's pleasance.
memoirs-and-historical-chronicles-of-the:
Memoirs and Historical Chronicles of the Courts of Europe joins three royal lives. Marguerite de Valois, wife of Henri IV, leads the set. Madame de Pompadour and Catherine de Medici stand with her.

Marguerite's letters open with tales of her infancy at court. Plots to turn her to the new faith fail, and she stays Catholic. A court progress and a grand festivity break off in sudden confusion. Her brother Anjou's plots and her loss of favor fill the next letters. A picture shows the child Mozart playing for Madame de Pompadour. Court art and court plots stand side by side in the set.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume one of Saint-Simon's memoirs of Louis XIV opens his set. The contents list for all fifteen volumes stands at the front. Chapter one gives his birth, his family, and his wish for the army.

He enters the Musketeers and serves at the siege of Namur. Chapter two treats the King's natural children and a forced royal wedding. The Duc de Chartres weds, and Madame rages at the match. Chapter three turns to his father's death and tales of Louis XIII. Anecdotes of Richelieu and Madame de Hautefort fill that chapter. Family pride and court favor shape the young duke's start.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book two of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs treats Philippe I first. Philippe II, the Regent, and his wife come next in the list. The Dauphine and Adelaide of Savoy stand in the heads as well.

Mazarin, she says, feared the King's brother would grow too learned. He told the tutor to let the boy play, not study. The brothers differed in all things: build, hair, taste, and temper. Monsieur loved dress, dance, and large parties more than the chase. He never rode, save with the army, and feared sun and powder. Her blunt portraits spare no one, kin least of all.
nasa-tm-19660027035-trajectory-optimizat:
Lyle R. Dickey, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this technical memorandum, dated May 25, 1966. Numbered TM X-53464, it tackles a core flight mechanics problem. It asks how to find the best possible path for a thrusting vehicle using step-by-step numerical methods.

Dickey starts from an assumed history of thrust direction and computes the path it produces. He then solves the linearized equations of motion directly for nearby paths. With that direct solution in hand, a planner can test whether the assumed path is truly the best one. The first and second variations together give a steady repeat-and-improve method for closing in on the optimum. The method keeps working even when the path includes sudden changes or limits partway through.
nasa-tm-19670009723-a-portable-different:
David Cleghorn, William A. Wall, and J. D. Bennight, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on December 5, 1966. It describes a shop tool: a portable gauge for measuring the inside flare angle of MC146 flared tubing. That angle is critical, because the tube must mate correctly with its fitting.

Quality control crews had been measuring the angle with plaster or plastic casts. That method was slow and costly. The new differential ball gauge measures the angle accurately and speedily instead. The memorandum includes the operating theory and the math behind the design, so other shops could build and trust the tool.
nasa-tm-19670022055-closed-loop-doppler-:
Peter E. O'Neill Jr., of the Communications Research Branch at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in June 1967. Based on his thesis at George Washington University, it presents a closed-loop Doppler correction scheme for satellite links. Motion between a satellite and a ground station shifts the received radio frequency, and precise work must remove that shift.

O'Neill's technique reduces the effective Doppler shift to roughly the second order of the velocity ratio, a far smaller error. Experimental data verified the method, matching theoretical predictions within three percent. A ground-controlled satellite clock of very high stability was established in the Relay II satellite using the scheme. Without correction, the frequency error could grow more than a thousand times larger. Analyses cover constant and changing velocity cases, plus a worst-case study for Relay II.
nasa-tm-19680011768-exploring-in-aerospa: Kirby W. Hiller, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, taught this lesson to the Lewis Aerospace Explorers in 1966 and 1967. It is chapter twenty-one of Exploring in Aerospace Rocketry, on biomedical engineering. The catalog record describes the topic as engineering methods put to work in medicine and biology. The hosted sample preserves the cover and series list only, with no readable lesson text.
nasa-tm-19680015962-hanging-chain-impact:
Wilmer H. Reed III of NASA's Langley Research Center describes a simple damper for tall, flexible structures in this paper, presented in Ottawa in September 1967. Wind makes antennas, stacks, and towers sway back and forth. That motion can damage structures or disrupt their work if nothing absorbs the energy.

Reed's damper is a chain covered with a rubber sleeve, hung beside a vertical channel. As the structure sways, the chain strikes the channel and soaks up energy. Tests measured how design choices changed the damper's performance. The results are given as mechanical admittance and related measures. The concept offers a cheap, simple fix for wind-driven shaking.
nasa-tm-19680017374-alloying-principles-:
G. Mervin Ault surveys alloying principles for heat resistant refractory metals in this July 1967 discussion supplement. The notes support a committee report on strengthening mechanisms. Refractory metals such as molybdenum, tungsten, and chromium promise strength at temperatures where normal alloys fail.

Ault reviews emerging alloy trends and the ductile to brittle transition, a key weakness of these metals. He discusses grain size effects and refractory metal fiber reinforced superalloys. Molybdenum alloys had reached transition temperatures below room temperature as produced, the notes state. Tungsten alloys still missed that goal in their strongest forms. The survey maps where alloy design stood and what designers still needed.
nasa-tm-19680024523-automatic-controls-f:
C. R. Nichols and S. J. Obloy of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52427, for a propulsion conference in Cleveland, Ohio. Their topic is automatic control of the test facilities and mercury ion thrusters used in long durability runs. Ion thrusters must fire for months to prove they can last, far longer than crews can watch them closely.

Three years of such tests at Lewis reshaped several vacuum chamber systems, the authors report. New controls allowed automatic shutdown during unattended running, protecting both thruster and chamber. Thruster control circuits let one person per shift keep tests running almost three months without pause. Further changes, they add, now permit fully unattended durability testing.
nasa-tm-19690021372-neutral-atmosphere-c:
Jimmy E. Cooley and Carl A. Reber wrote this June 1969 Goddard preprint, numbered X-621-69-276. They report neutral atmosphere composition measured between about one hundred thirty and five hundred thirty kilometers up. A magnetic mass spectrometer flew on the Geoprobe, a Javelin rocket launched from Wallops Island, Virginia, on March 2, 1966.

The sealed instrument opened to the air by a pyrotechnic device once aloft. Helium and nitrogen readings agreed well with the standard model above two hundred fifty kilometers, they report. Measured oxygen values in the lower thermosphere ran below the model's, however. Working from the nitrogen profile, they place the exospheric temperature near nine hundred degrees for that flight.
nasa-tm-19710024241-discontinuities-in-t:
L. F. Burlaga of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this study in August 1971, numbered X-691-71-327, on discontinuities in the interplanetary medium. These are sharp boundaries in the solar wind where the magnetic field and plasma change abruptly. Burlaga connects them to how cosmic rays spread through space and gain energy.

Recent electron temperature measurements show magnetic and thermal pressures are about equal in the solar wind. That means hydromagnetic theory, not plain fluid theory, must describe these boundaries. Observations show most interplanetary magnetic discontinuities are tangential, lying along the field. Forward and reverse fast shocks and slow shocks have all been observed, and forward fast shocks can raise particle energies several fold. Fermi acceleration of particles trapped between a shock and magnetic fluctuations can explain the observations.
no-name:
Wilkie Collins built No Name in an unusual shape, as its contents page shows. Instead of plain parts, the novel runs in scenes, like a play. Chapters sit inside each scene, numbered fresh as the scene changes. Between the scenes come short interludes with that very title.

The sampled contents run from the first scene through the fourth and beyond. A preface stands before the first scene opens. Collins, known for tales of secrets and schemes, here borrows the stage's frame. Scene changes let time pass and letters or reports fill the gaps. Readers who like his mysteries get the same grip in a new form.
notable-women-of-olden-time:
Written for the American Sunday-School Union, Notable Women of Olden Time was entered at Philadelphia in 1852. No author is named. The union, at 1122 Chestnut Street, printed it under a committee drawn from seven church bodies. No book of theirs could pass if any committee member objected.

The contents sort Bible women by a trait or a role. Sarah is the wife, and Hagar the wife unloved. Rebekah is the partial and intriguing mother. Leah and Rachel are the rival sisters, and Miriam the affectionate sister. Deborah is the prophetess, and Jezebel the artful woman. Sunday school readers got scripture lives as lessons in character.
on-the-sublime:
Longinus is the name attached to this ancient critical treatise. H. L. Havell translated it into English prose. Andrew Lang wrote the introduction to this edition. Macmillan published it in London in 1890. The translator dedicates his attempt to Professor Butcher of Edinburgh.

The treatise asks what makes writing grand and moving. The sublime lifts readers beyond mere persuasion or pleasure. Longinus studies great passages from Greek and Roman authors. He links grandeur of thought with grandeur of style. Scholars still debate who truly wrote the work. It remains a founding text of literary criticism. Havell's version made it plain for English readers.
once-upon-a-time:
Richard Harding Davis gathered these short stories in 1912. Scribner's published the book in New York that year. Davis dedicated the volume to Gouverneur Morris. The contents list eight tales of adventure and society. Titles include The Spy, The Messengers, and A Charmed Life.

Other tales treat latitude, wasted days, and peace maneuvers. The Amateur and The Make-Believe Man close the list. Davis was famed as a war reporter and storyteller. His tales move fast, with polish and charm. Settings range from drawing rooms to foreign posts. The book shows his popular short fiction at its best.
one-day-s-courtship-and-the-heralds-of-f:
Robert Barr wrote these two tales, published in 1896. Artist John Trenton opens the first tale with a letter. He sails for England on the twenty-seventh, he writes. First he must revisit Shawenegan Falls in Canada. Their roar has stayed in his ears since leaving.

Trenton asks his friend to reserve a canoe for Tuesday. Two expert guides must take him up and back safely. His sketches failed, so he will bring a camera. The second tale, The Heralds of Fame, follows it. Barr writes crisp, witty fiction with Canadian color. The courtship of the title unfolds within one day.
one-man-in-his-time:
Ellen Glasgow published this novel in the year 1922. A note says no character was drawn from real people. The title quotes Shakespeare on man playing many parts. Chapter one is called The Shadow, chapter two Gideon Vetch. Corinna of the old print shop enters in chapter three.

Later chapters send Corinna to war and Patty into society. Old walls and a rising tide frame the change. A journey into mean streets tests the characters. Glasgow writes about old Virginia meeting a new age. September roses and magic soften her social satire. The book suits readers of thoughtful American fiction.

pe-lle-as-and-me-lisande-alladine-and-pa:
Maurice Maeterlinck's volume gathers three of his plays in Richard Hovey's English translation: Pélléas and Mélisande, Alladine and Palomides, and Home. Maeterlinck's own preface, printed in French, asks whether his dramas were truly written for a marionette theatre, as he once claimed.

He answers that they were not written for ordinary actors, and argues that poems die when living beings step into them. The preface sets out his symbolist theory of drama before the plays begin. Pélléas and Mélisande, the doomed love story that leads the volume, later became famous through the music it inspired.

poems-of-the-heart-and-home: Mrs. J. C. Yule's verses celebrate the domestic affections — home, children, friendship, and faith — in the gentle style Victorian readers cherished. Her poems were written for the family circle, to be read aloud and treasured. A sweet, sincere collection from an age that honored the poetry of everyday love.
reflections-on-the-decline-of-science-in: Charles Babbage's 1830 polemic against the sorry state of British science, by the man who designed the first computer. The inventor of the Difference Engine blasts the Royal Society's cronyism and calls for real support of research. Cantankerous, brilliant, and historically important, it helped reform British science.
returning-home: Returning Home is a moving story of homecoming and reckoning. Its weary traveler comes back at last to face the past. Old ties pull hard against newly learned ways. A quiet and thoughtful tale of return.
sima-qian-memoires-historiques-chavannes:
Édouard Chavannes spent a decade turning Sima Qian's Shiji into French, and his fifth tome, from 1905, holds chapters forty-three through forty-seven. The Shiji itself dates to about 91 BCE and is the founding work of Chinese history writing. An index and errata close the French volume.

These chapters give biographies, the lives of men whose deeds shaped the early Han world. Chavannes filled his pages with notes on names, places, and rites, drawn from Chinese commentaries. His version was the standard Western Shiji for a century. Readers of French meet the grand historian here with a sure guide at their side.

Chapters thirty-one through forty-two of the Shiji fill the fourth tome of Édouard Chavannes's French translation, printed in 1901. Sima Qian's history, from about 91 BCE, here moves through the great houses and into the lives. The French text carries Chavannes's dense notes throughout.

The hereditary houses tell of the old feudal states and the families that ruled them for the Zhou kings. Then the biographies begin, lives of ministers and men of mark. Chavannes used Chinese commentaries to pin down names and dates. His set remains the fullest Western version of the grand historian made in the public domain era.

The third tome of Édouard Chavannes's French Shiji, from 1898, holds chapters thirteen through twenty-two. Sima Qian compiled the Records of the Grand Historian around 91 BCE. This stretch of the work is its frame: the tables and the first of the hereditary houses.

Chronological tables line up the rulers of the states year by year, so the reader can see who held power when. Then the houses begin, the long family tales of Zhou's feudal lords. Chavannes explains the tables with notes drawn from Chinese scholarship. Dry as they look, these pages are the spine of the whole Shiji.

the-game: Jack London's 1905 novel about a young boxer fighting for the money to marry his sweetheart. Told with brutal realism and deep sympathy, it is both a love story and a condemnation of the prize ring. Short, powerful, and heartbreaking, it is London's best boxing fiction.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio: Macaulay's famous History opens with James II taking the throne in 1685 and sweeps through the Glorious Revolution that threw him out. Whig history at its most brilliant: confident, vivid, and gloriously readable, it made the past feel like breaking news. The book that taught Victorian England its own story.
the-honor-of-the-name: The Honor of the Name, Émile Gaboriau's novel. The family's honor. This book preserves that tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.

the-lady-of-blossholme: Haggard's The Lady of Blossholme is set in Reformation England. A brave lady defies a cruel abbot and his grasping monks. Peril and pageantry fill the Tudor adventure. A stirring historical romance of Tudor England.
the-little-shepherd-of-kingdom-come: John Fox Jr.'s beloved 1903 novel about Chad, the Kentucky mountain boy, and his passage through the Civil War. Tender, patriotic, and hugely popular in its day, it was a bestseller for years. A classic of Southern fiction.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: In his second book the young Casanova takes to the open road. Fresh towns bring him fresh scrapes and fresh loves. The great lover’s own tale gathers speed. The great lover’s own tale gathers speed.
